newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore unit trusts need insurance -Chubb.
newsitem.headline: Singapore unit trusts need insurance -Chubb.

text.p: Chubb Corp's Singapore unit said on Monday a boom in unit trust investments had raised the need for insurance to cover trusts, asset managers and trustees from increasingly volatile markets and potential litigation.
"Liabilities do exist and a need (for insurance) is there because the liability is there," said Charles Szvetecz, Chubb Group assistant vice president and Asia Pacific zone manager.
He was speaking at a news conference launching a unit trust asset protection insurance programme underwritten by Chubb unit Federal Insurance Company.

Szvetecz said as Singapore became the regional focus of the unit trust and asset management market, competitive pressures would grow that could lead to disputes as investors became more sophisticated and scrutinised trust activity more closely.
"When you get this heightened activity along with it comes a lot of competition and volatility," he said.
Singapore has about 80 unit trusts which among them have about Singapore $3.0 billion under management. Taking the broader asset management picture, there is about S$125 billion under management.

"If we don't see a growth in the number of companies we'll certainly see a substantial rise in the amount of funds under management in the next few years," Svetecz added, but declined to give a forecast.

He said the development of the Singapore asset management market could draw parallels with those of the UK and the U.S. where demand for insurance products to protect funds, managers and trustees already existed.
"We know there is an inherent demand here," he said.
The Chubb product, to be launched in Hong Kong and Australia by the end of the year, can provide cover on three levels to a total of US$10 million per policy.

It can cover trustees for their legal liabilities in overseeing the trust, it can cover asset managers administering the funds, and it can indemnify the fund itself for costs it may incur resulting from the actions of its managers or trustees.
Chubb, which began researching the product a year ago, said issues of corporate governance and fiduciary duty were gaining prominence around Asia, and in Singapore specifically.
"The liabilities do exist. We haven't seen any occurrences (in the courts) yet, but the liability is there," Szvetecz said.
